  • whereq.cloud —— 加油站及其实时油价、聚合价格序列，以及行政区划：省、区域、市镇、城市、城镇、ward、neighbourhood，还带着它们真实的边界轮廓。
  • OpenStreetMap —— 你身边的地点。咖啡、餐饮、停车、药房、walk-in clinic、广场、图书馆。
  • RSS 与 JSON 信息源 —— 也就是地图右上角可以开关的那些本地新闻、活动、故事与话题。

一个账号，一把 key，一份速率配额。whereq.cloud 的 API 每分钟允许 30 次请求，所以两条 whereq.cloud 爬虫共用同一个限流器——两个各自独立的限流器各放行 30 次/分，只会互相把对方顶成 429。它按 coverage target 轮转（一个国家、一个省、一座城市、一个地图视口），所以单次 tick 绝不会向数据源讨要整块大陆；某个 target 失败了，会在下一个 tick 重试，而不是干等一个间隔。

内容爬虫是同一个思路，只是多接了一个解析器：从登记在册的信息源里发现条目，做归一化，抽出地点，用一条 provider 链反查坐标，分类，然后 upsert 进数据库。某条信息源失联时，它只会把该源的 last_status 记为 error，整轮抓取照常继续。

whereq.com​

多伦多市中心。左侧：neighbourhood 指南、本地必备、快捷分类；再往下是图层——行政区划、隐患、精选指南、好友、每日路线。右上角：爬虫从信息源拉回来的内容。

whereq.com 是一个以地图为中心的地点平台。打开它，你看到身边的地点；再打开其中任何一个，得到的是一页完整资料——地址、营业时间、分类、照片、到那里的路线，以及人们留下的笔记。

今天它能做的事包括：

  • 地点与附近搜索 —— POI 地图，加上一个把半径内所有东西合并成单一排序列表的附近搜索。
  • 地点卡片 —— 每个地点一页完整页面，由人来写，不是由信息源生成的。
  • 学校 —— 覆盖范围内的每一所学校，连同它的学区边界，直接画在地图上。
  • 隐患 —— 环境与基础设施隐患，标注在地图上，也允许上报。
  • 油价 —— 加油站与实时价格，从 whereq.cloud 爬来。
  • 地理 —— 把地点「装进去」的那些区域，带真实轮廓。
  • 路线、好友、收藏地点、通知 —— 一张地图应用该有的那些社交部分。
  • 英文、法文与简体中文，贯穿整个界面。

技术说明​

  • 前端 —— React 18、TypeScript、Vite、Tailwind。类型检查是严格的（noUnusedLocals、noUnusedParameters），它也是前端唯一真正的关卡。
  • 后端 —— FastAPI、SQLAlchemy、Pydantic，18 个 Alembic migration。
  • 数据库 —— PostgreSQL 17 + PostGIS。真正的 geometry 列、GiST 索引，以及不会被简化边界骗过的点在多边形内判定。
  • 许可 —— MIT，覆盖整个仓库，包括爬虫。
  • 测试 —— 235 个，不需要数据库，也不需要网络；少数几个需要真实 Postgres 的用例是可选开启的。

这篇文章不是文档。 文档是仓库本身：安装指南、爬虫指南、库表结构、数据来源及其许可。我更希望你直接去读那些，而不是听我一面之词。

👉 github.com/whereq/WhereQ-com

跑起来：

git clone https://github.com/whereq/WhereQ-com.git
cd WhereQ-com
cp docker/.env.example docker/.env
# 设置 POSTGRES_PASSWORD 和 SECRET_KEY
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --build

这就是完整的一栈——带 PostGIS 的 PostgreSQL、migration、API、爬虫，以及由 nginx 托管的前端。启动后访问 localhost:3743。

构建、测试、运行都不需要任何 key。 把 OIDC 留空，它就以匿名模式运行，登录入口自动隐藏；把 whereq.cloud 的 key 留空，油价面板就是空的，地理数据则回落到它的公开层。Google Maps 的 key 只决定地图本身画不画得出来。

为什么现在把它放出来​

这个仓库只有 一个 commit。

这不是失误，也不是从模板起的新项目。我在发布前重写了它的历史，因为这个应用的历史里，藏着一些本来就不该离开我电脑的东西——凭据字面量、一场许可证明确不允许再分发的学校数据实验、还有我写给自己看的部署笔记。git 历史是一份永久的公开记录，事情发生之后再删掉一行，并不能把已经泄露的东西收回来。

所以历史被重写，私人的东西从每一个 commit 里清了出去，公开出来的只剩代码、migration、CI 和文档。旧的 commit 不存在于任何读者能触及的地方。

再往下一层，理由其实更朴素：这张地图是整个 WhereQ Universe 里其他应用要读的那一块。它本来就在对外提供一个带密钥的地理编码 API——geocode、autocomplete、反查、路线、matrix、静态地图——好让同门的其他应用不必自己持有 Google key。既然大家都要依赖这个服务，那么它背后的爬虫、以及这张地图本身，就应该让任何想自己跑一份的人读得到。

如果你想为自己所在的城市跑一份自己的地图，这是一份起点，不是一个成品。拿走吧。

致谢​

这个应用站在别人的劳动之上，装作不是那样才是不诚实的。

  • whereq.cloud —— 我们自己的数据平台。加油站、实时油价、价格序列和行政区划都由它提供，本应用负责爬取。油价数据是授权且计费的；地理数据则是开放数据。
  • OpenStreetMap 的贡献者们 —— POI 图层、neighbourhood 几何，以及人口普查分区，采用 ODbL 1.0。署名信息随每一行数据一起走，页脚里也有。
  • geoBoundaries —— 正式的行政边界，采用 CC-BY 4.0。
  • Google Maps Platform —— 地图本身、作为兜底的地理编码和路线规划。他们的署名格式是每一个地图界面都必须带的，应用里已经带上。
  • geocode.maps.co、LocationIQ、Geocodio、Nominatim —— 免费的几档地理编码服务，排付费 provider 前面试，这样付费额度只在前面全都用尽时才会被消耗。
  • feedparser，以及构建这个仓库所依赖的整个 Python 与 JavaScript 生态。完整清单在 NOTICE 里。

也要谢谢那些告诉我图钉画错了、药店漏掉了、油价过期了的人：这张地图之所以更好，是因为你们说它不好。

如果你自己跑起了一份，或者为你的城市改造了它——我很想听听。

entry.title: whereq.com is open source — the map, the crawler, and everything it reads
entry.content:
A pin is a very small sentence​

Stand on a street in Toronto and look at the address in front of you. A map gives you one claim about it: there is a pin here. A coffee shop. A hospital. A school. Maybe a parking garage.

But the place itself is a pile of claims, and the pin is the least interesting one of them.

Which school catchment is that address in? Can I walk to a library, and which one? Is the fuel station on the corner charging 1.42or1.42 or 1.42or1.79? Is that building inside a ward, or inside a neighbourhood, or in a ward and a neighbourhood? Did anything happen on this street last week?

Every one of those answers is a piece of data, and every one of them lives somewhere else. The school boundaries are in one system, the fuel prices in another, the administrative outlines in a third, the local news in a fourth. The map you are looking at is the result of all of them agreeing.

So I built the part that agrees​

The thing that surprised me while building it was how much of the work was not the map at all.

Drawing pins is the easy half. The hard half is that a map is a join. Every layer needs its own key, its own licence, its own rate limit, its own idea of what a place is — and a POI (a point at an address) is not the same thing as an administrative area (a polygon that contains an address), no matter how casually you can slide one into the other.

So the first version of this app had three different ingestion scripts, each one written for its own dataset, each one holding its own API key, each one breaking on its own schedule.

That is the shape of the problem, and it is a shape almost every application in the world has: ten apps, ten scrapers, ten nightly failures.

The fix was to make the retrieval a layer of its own — one process, one cadence, one place where the outside world is allowed to enter the app.

I call it the crawler, and it is the part of this repository I am most pleased with.

The crawler​

Everything on the map arrives by being crawled:

  • whereq.cloud — fuel stations and their live prices, the aggregated price series, and the administrative geography: provinces, regions, municipalities, cities, towns, wards and neighbourhoods, with their real outlines.
  • OpenStreetMap — the places around you. Coffee, food, parking, pharmacies, walk-in clinics, plazas, libraries.
  • RSS and JSON feeds — the local news, events, stories and topics that you can switch on in the top-right corner of the map.

One account, one key, one rate limit. The whereq.cloud API allows 30 requests a minute, so the two whereq.cloud crawls share a single throttle — two independent limiters would each allow 30/min and would throttle each other into 429s. It rotates through coverage targets round-robin (a country, a province, a city, a map viewport) so a single tick never asks the upstream for a whole continent, and a target that failed is retried on the next tick rather than waiting out its interval.

The content crawler is the same idea with a parser attached: it discovers items from the registered sources, normalizes them, extracts the location, geocodes it through a provider chain, classifies them, and upserts them. A feed that goes dark records last_status='error' and the crawl carries on.

whereq.com​

Downtown Toronto. On the left: the neighbourhood guide, the local essentials, the quick categories. Below that: the layers — administrative areas, hazards, curated guides, friends, daily routes. Top right: the content the crawler pulled from the feeds.

whereq.com is a map-centric location platform. Open it and you see the places around you; open any one of them and you get a proper page — address, hours, categories, photos, the route to it, and the notes people left.

Some of what it does today:

  • Places and nearby — a POI map, plus a nearby search that merges everything within a radius into one ranked list.
  • Place cards — a full page per place, written by people, not by a feed.
  • Schools — every school in the coverage area with its catchment boundary, drawn on the map.
  • Hazards — environmental and infrastructure hazards, mapped and reported.
  • Fuel — stations and live prices, crawled from whereq.cloud.
  • Geography — the areas that contain the places, with real outlines.
  • Routes, friends, saved places, notifications — the ordinary social parts of a map app.
  • English, French and Simplified Chinese, throughout.

The honest technical note​

  • Frontend — React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind. The typecheck is strict (noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters), and it is the only real gate the frontend has.
  • Backend — FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, 18 Alembic migrations.
  • Database — PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS. Real geometry columns, a GiST index, and point-in-polygon tests that are not fooled by a simplified edge.
  • Licence — MIT, for the whole repository, including the crawler.
  • Tests — 235 of them, and they need no database and no network. The handful that want a live Postgres are opt-in.

This post is not the documentation. The documentation is the repository: the setup guide, the crawler guide, the schema, the data sources and their licences. I would rather you read those than take my word for it.

👉 github.com/whereq/WhereQ-com

To run it:

git clone https://github.com/whereq/WhereQ-com.git
cd WhereQ-com
cp docker/.env.example docker/.env
# set POSTGRES_PASSWORD and SECRET_KEY
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --build

That is the whole stack — PostgreSQL with PostGIS, the migrations, the API, the crawler and the nginx-served frontend. It comes up on localhost:3743.

You do not need any keys to build, test or run it. Leave the OIDC provider empty and it runs in anonymous mode with the sign-in control hidden. Leave the whereq.cloud key empty and the fuel panels stay empty and the geography feed falls back to its public tier. The Google Maps key only decides whether the map itself draws.

Why it is in the world now​

The repository has one commit.

That is not an accident, and it is not a fresh start from a template. I rewrote the history before publishing it, because the history of this app contained things that were never meant to leave my machine — credential literals, an experiment with school data whose licence forbids redistribution, notes to myself about a deployment. A git history is a permanent public record, and deleting a line after the fact does not un-burn it.

So the history was rewritten, the private things were purged from every commit, and what is published is the code, the migrations, the CI and the documentation. The old commits do not exist anywhere a reader can reach them.

Beyond that, the honest reason is simpler: this map is the piece the rest of the universe reads. It already serves a keyed geocoding API — geocode, autocomplete, reverse geocode, routes, matrix, static maps — so sibling applications can geocode without holding a Google key of their own. If that service is going to be depended on by other people, then the crawler behind it, and the map itself, should be readable by anyone who wants to run their own.

If you want to run your own map of your own city, this is a starting point, not a finished product. Take it.

Credits​

This app stands on the work of other people, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

  • whereq.cloud — our own data platform. It provides the fuel stations, the live prices, the price series and the administrative geography this app crawls. The fuel data is licensed and metered; the geography feed is open data.
  • OpenStreetMap contributors — the POI layer, the neighbourhood geometry, and the census subdivisions, under the ODbL 1.0. The attribution travels with every row, and the footer carries it.
  • geoBoundaries — the formal administrative boundaries, under CC-BY 4.0.
  • Google Maps Platform — the map itself, the geocoding fallback and the routing. Their attribution string is required on every map surface and is in the app.
  • geocode.maps.co, LocationIQ, Geocodio and Nominatim — the free geocoding tiers that are tried before the paid provider, so the paid quota is spent only when everything else is exhausted.
  • feedparser and the rest of the Python and JavaScript ecosystems that this repository is built on. The full list is in NOTICE.

And to everyone who has reported a wrong pin, a missing pharmacy or a stale price: the map is better because you told me it was wrong.

If you run your own copy, or fork it for your own city — I would genuinely like to hear about it.

entry.title: Inside the WhereQ Universe: One Identity, Many Apps, Open APIs
entry.summary: The WhereQ Universe is not a single product — it is a
entry.content:
The WhereQ Universe is not a single product — it is a living ecosystem of independent applications that share one identity layer, one set of engineering conventions, and an increasingly open set of APIs. This post walks through how the pieces fit together: why authentication lives in a single place, how the apps expose data to customers, and where LLM agents and MCP fit into the picture.

The family at a glance​

Every application in the Universe is deployable and operable on its own, but none of them re-implement the cross-cutting concerns that every SaaS needs. Instead, those concerns are factored out into shared services.

ApplicationDomainWhat it does
WhereQ App Hubwhereq.caThe Universe entry point — a decentralized hub that ties the family together.
Key To Marvelkeytomarvel.comCentralized identity & access management (OAuth/OIDC provider).
FlowDeskflowdesk.topAI-powered stock analysis backed by a large archive of market records.
CatoBigatocatobigato.comAI tutor for K‑12 through college.
Chroniqchroniq.ccTime/records-oriented application in the family.
WhereQ LLMwhereq.ccAI/LLM-integrated platform (in progress).
WhereQwhereq.comLocation-based guides, stories, and this engineering blog.

The guiding idea is simple: build each app small, and never duplicate a capability that the ecosystem can provide once. The two most important shared capabilities today are identity (Key To Marvel) and data/agent access (the open APIs and LLM wikis exposed by FlowDesk, CatoBigato, and Chroniq).

Key To Marvel: one OAuth provider for the whole Universe​

Historically, every new application meant re-solving the same problem: user registration, login, password reset, social login, token issuance, session management, role and permission modelling. Copy-pasting an auth module into each codebase is how you end up with five slightly different, slightly broken login systems and five places to patch when a CVE lands.

Key To Marvel eliminates that duplication. It is the single, centralized OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect provider for the entire Universe. When a new application needs authentication, it does not build an auth module. It simply creates a realm in Key To Marvel and points its login flow there.

                         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
                         │            Key To Marvel                 │
                         │        (keytomarvel.com — IdP)           │
                         │                                          │
                         │   ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐             │
                         │   │  realm:  │  │  realm:  │   ...       │
                         │   │ flowdesk │  │ catobi.  │             │
                         │   └──────────┘  └──────────┘             │
                         │      OAuth2 / OIDC · JWT · social login  │
                         └───────────────▲──────────────────────────┘
                                         │  OIDC redirect + token
             ┌───────────────┬───────────┴───────────┬───────────────┐
             │               │                       │               │
       ┌────────────┐   ┌───────────┐          ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐
       │ FlowDesk   │   │ CatoBigato│          │  Chroniq  │   │ WhereQ ×N │
       │flowdesk.top│   │catobigato │          │chroniq.cc │   │  apps     │
       └────────────┘   └───────────┘          └───────────┘   └───────────┘
        each app = one realm; no app ships its own auth module

Why a realm-per-application model​

A realm is an isolated security domain: its own users, roles, clients, and token policies. Giving each application its own realm buys us several things at once:

  • Isolation. FlowDesk's users, roles, and clients never leak into CatoBigato's. A misconfiguration in one realm cannot affect another.
  • Zero duplication. Login, registration, MFA, password reset, social login, token refresh, and session revocation are implemented once and inherited by every app that has a realm.
  • Consistent tokens. Every app validates the same kind of signed JWT against Key To Marvel's public keys (JWKS). Backend services just verify the token — they never store passwords.
  • Central policy & patching. Password rules, token lifetimes, brute-force protection, and security patches are applied in one place and take effect everywhere.
  • Optional SSO. Because all realms live behind one provider, single sign-on across family apps is a configuration decision, not a rewrite.

What an app has to do​

Onboarding a new application to the Universe's identity layer is intentionally boring:

  1. Create a realm (or client within a shared realm) in Key To Marvel.
  2. Register the app's redirect URIs and obtain a client ID/secret.
  3. Wire the standard OIDC login flow — redirect to Key To Marvel, receive the authorization code, exchange it for tokens.
  4. Validate the resulting JWT on the backend using Key To Marvel's JWKS.

That's it. No user table, no password hashing, no reset-email plumbing. The application focuses entirely on its own domain.

User ──▶ App (flowdesk.top)
          │  1. not authenticated → redirect
          ▼
     Key To Marvel  ── 2. login / social login / MFA ──▶ user authenticates
          │
          │  3. authorization code → app callback
          ▼
     App exchanges code ──▶ Key To Marvel ──▶ 4. access + refresh JWT
          │
          ▼
     App backend verifies JWT signature via JWKS → grants access

Open APIs: making integration easy for customers​

Identity is only half of the "don't duplicate" story. The other half is data and capability access. Several applications in the Universe already provide — or are actively building — public API access so that customers can integrate without scraping UIs or reverse-engineering internals.

  • FlowDesk — API access for stock data and analysis (details below).
  • CatoBigato — API access to its tutoring and explanation capabilities.
  • Chroniq — API access to its records/timeline capabilities.

The goal is to turn each app from a walled garden into a building block: customers should be able to pull the data or trigger the functionality they need directly, and compose it into their own products.

LLM wikis for agents and MCP​

APIs make integration possible; LLM wikis make integration effortless. Alongside their REST endpoints, FlowDesk, CatoBigato, and Chroniq are providing LLM wikis — structured, machine-readable documentation designed to be consumed by an LLM agent or exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Instead of a human reading API docs and hand-writing an integration, an LLM agent can ingest the wiki, understand the available endpoints, their parameters, and their semantics, and then call them directly. In practice this means:

  • An agent can discover what an app can do and how to ask for it without a developer translating docs into code.
  • An MCP server can front the app's API, so any MCP-capable assistant can use FlowDesk, CatoBigato, or Chroniq as a tool.
  • Integration shifts from "read docs → write client → maintain client" to "point an agent at the wiki."
   ┌──────────────┐        reads        ┌──────────────────┐
   │  LLM Agent   │ ──────────────────> │   LLM Wiki       │
   │  / MCP host  │                     │ (app-provided)   │
   └──────┬───────┘                     └──────────────────┘
          │  calls, guided by the wiki
          ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  App API  (flowdesk.top / catobigato / chroniq)│
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

FlowDesk: a market-data archive you can query​

FlowDesk deserves a closer look because it sits on top of a genuinely valuable asset: a large, accumulated archive of stock records collected from various stock markets. Over time FlowDesk has been ingesting and storing market data across exchanges, building up historical depth that most integrations would find expensive to reproduce.

That archive is being opened up. FlowDesk will provide endpoints (and other mechanisms) for customers to fetch stock records directly — so instead of sourcing, cleaning, and warehousing market data yourself, you can pull it from FlowDesk and get straight to the analysis.

   Various stock markets ──▶ FlowDesk ingestion ──▶ Stock-records archive
                                                          │
                                    ┌─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
                                    ▼                     ▼                       ▼
                              Customer API           LLM wiki / MCP        FlowDesk's own
                              (fetch records)        (agent access)        AI analysis

Combined with the LLM wiki, this is the pattern the whole Universe is moving toward: accumulate something valuable once, then expose it through both a human-friendly API and an agent-friendly wiki.

How it all fits together​

Put the two shared layers side by side and the architecture of the Universe becomes clear:

                        ┌────────────────────────────────┐
                        │        WhereQ App Hub          │
                        │          (whereq.ca)           │
                        └───────────────┬────────────────┘
                                        │
        ┌───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┐
        │                               │                               │
  ┌───────────┐                   ┌───────────┐                   ┌───────────┐
  │ FlowDesk  │                   │ CatoBigato│                   │  Chroniq  │
  │  + API    │                   │  + API    │                   │  + API    │
  │  + wiki   │                   │  + wiki   │                   │  + wiki   │
  └─────┬─────┘                   └─────┬─────┘                   └─────┬─────┘
        │                               │                               │
        └───────────── authenticate via OIDC ───────────────────────────┘
                                        │
                                        ▼
                        ┌────────────────────────────────┐
                        │         Key To Marvel          │
                        │   centralized OAuth / OIDC     │
                        │      (one realm per app)       │
                        └────────────────────────────────┘

Two rules capture the design philosophy:

  1. Authenticate once, everywhere. No application in the Universe builds its own auth. Each one creates a realm in Key To Marvel and trusts its tokens.
  2. Expose what you accumulate. Apps that gather valuable data or capabilities (FlowDesk's market archive, CatoBigato's tutoring, Chroniq's records) publish them through open APIs and LLM wikis, so both developers and AI agents can integrate with minimal friction.

The result is an ecosystem where new applications are cheap to launch — they inherit identity for free and can lean on the family's data and services — while customers get a consistent login experience and a growing catalog of APIs and agent-ready integrations.

Explore the full ecosystem at whereq.ca.

entry.title: Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw：全面对比
entry.content:
Hermes

vs🦞 OpenClaw

从所有维度进行全面深度对比 — 架构、安全、记忆、技能、平台、成本等
更新于 2026 年 4 月

01 起源与哲学02 架构设计03 学习与自我进化04 记忆系统05 技能生态06 消息平台支持07 模型支持08 安全性09 部署与基础设施10 开发者体验11 成本分析12 社区与生态13 企业与团队使用14 研究能力15 迁移路径16 最终结论

01 起源与哲学

图 1：两种截然不同的理念 — Hermes 押注认知深度，OpenClaw 押注连接广度。

OpenClaw 定义了个人 AI 智能体品类。最初名为 Clawdbot（2025 年 11 月），因商标问题先后改名为 Moltbot 和 OpenClaw。创始人 Peter Steinberger 于 2026 年 2 月加入 OpenAI，项目转由非营利基金会社区治理。

Hermes Agent 两个月后由 Nous Research 发布 — 该实验室是 Hermes、Nomos、Psyche 模型家族的创造者。OpenClaw 优化的是连接尽可能多的平台和工具，而 Hermes 优化的是深度：让智能体通过使用真正学习和进化。

02 架构设计

图 2：Hermes 以 Agent 循环为中心；OpenClaw 以 Gateway 控制平面为中心。
维度 Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
核心AIAgent 循环（Python，约 9,200 行）Gateway 控制平面（Node.js/TS）
入口hermes（CLI）+ hermes gatewayopenclaw CLI + Gateway 守护进程
状态存储SQLite + FTS5 + 扁平文件JSON 配置 + 工作区文件
协议直接 LLM API 调用WebSocket 控制平面
插件模型Python 工具 + MCP 服务器Node.js 技能 + ClawHub 注册表
技术栈PythonNode.js / TypeScript

03 学习与自我进化 HERMES 胜出

这是最大的差异化特性。Hermes 拥有其他智能体框架无法复制的闭环学习循环。OpenClaw 的技能是静态的 — 你写了它们，除非手动更新，否则永远不变。

图 3：Hermes 自主创建并改进技能；OpenClaw 完全依赖人工编写的静态技能。
能力 Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
技能创建复杂任务后自主创建（5+ 工具调用）仅手动（人工编写 SKILL.md）
技能改进使用过程中自我改进无（静态文件）
用户建模Honcho 辩证建模，跨会话积累SOUL.md 静态身份文件

跨会话召回FTS5 搜索 + LLM 摘要按助手持久记忆
实测改进重复任务速度提升 40%无复利效果

04 记忆系统 HERMES 胜出

层级 Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
持久事实MEMORY.md（约 2,200 字符，会话开始冻结）按助手存储记忆
用户画像USER.md（偏好、风格）SOUL.md（身份和人格）
程序性知识技能库（自动创建、可搜索）技能（人工编写、静态）
情景记忆SQLite + FTS5 全文搜索，无限量按助手的会话持久化
摘要LLM 驱动的历史会话摘要无等效功能
外部提供商7 个可插拔提供商（Hindsight、PLUR 等）无可插拔记忆系统

Hermes 将记忆视为分层系统：始终在上下文中的事实、按需加载的程序性技能、可搜索的情景历史。OpenClaw 的记忆更简单但对团队隔离有效 — 每个助手有自己独立的存储，防止多代理设置中的交叉污染。

05 技能生态 OPENCLAW 胜出

OpenClaw 的生态系统在绝对数量上远超 Hermes。ClawHub 有数千个社区技能，覆盖从 Gmail 到 Kubernetes 的各种场景。但这种规模带来了严重的安全代价 — ClawHavoc 供应链攻击和 1,467+ 确认的恶意技能代表严重的信任问题。Hermes 用广度换安全：更少的技能，但有预执行扫描和更安全的默认姿态。

OpenClaw 支持 LINE、Google Chat、Microsoft Teams、IRC、Twitch、Nostr、Zalo 以及原生 iOS/Android/macOS 配套应用 — Hermes 目前均不支持。Hermes 的优势在于跨平台对话连续性（语义上下文恢复）和更深的单平台集成（Discord 语音频道、Telegram Webhook 模式、企业微信 WebSocket）。

07 模型支持 HERMES 胜出

08 安全性 HERMES 胜出

这是对比中最触目惊心的部分。OpenClaw 经历了 2026 年最严重的 AI 安全危机之一。

Hermes 的 Serverless 后端（Modal、Daytona）对于不需要 24/7 运行智能体的用户来说具有显著成本优势。如果你的智能体每天运行 8 小时，你只为 8 小时付费，而不是 24 小时。

12 社区与生态 OPENCLAW 胜出

指标 Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

能力 Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

Hermes 由模型训练实验室构建，从一开始就设计为研究基础设施 — 不仅仅是面向用户的产品。OpenClaw 没有等效的研究能力。

15 迁移路径

OpenClaw → Hermes：内置迁移工具

hermes claw migrate 可导入你的人格（SOUL.md）、记忆、技能（自动转换为 agentskills.io 格式）、消息平台配置、API 密钥和 TTS 资源。支持交互式预览和 dry-run。技能冲突通过 skip/overwrite/rename 选项处理。可以在过渡期间同时运行两个代理。

🦞 Hermes → OpenClaw：手动过程

无内置迁移工具。需要手动映射记忆文件、技能格式转换和频道重新配置。自我进化技能系统在 OpenClaw 中没有等效物 — 你会失去复利自动化价值。预估工作量：12–21 小时。

16 最终结论

图 4：14 个对比维度的逐类别胜出汇总。

选择 Hermes 当你...

  • 希望智能体随时间真正变得更强
  • 优先考虑安全性（零 CVE，Docker 默认加固）
  • 需要数月交互的深度记忆
  • 想要 Serverless 部署，空闲近零成本
  • 使用中国 LLM 提供商（MiniMax、GLM、Kimi）
  • 是需要 RL 训练 / 轨迹生成的研究者
  • 想从 OpenClaw 迁移（内置迁移工具）

🦞 选择 OpenClaw 当你...

  • 需要最广泛的平台覆盖（25+）
  • 想要庞大的技能生态（ClawHub 13,700+）
  • 需要企业支持（NVIDIA NemoClaw）
  • 需要原生 Windows 支持
  • 想要配套应用（macOS、iOS、Android）
  • 需要多代理路由和按助手数据隔离
  • 已有成熟的 OpenClaw 部署
🤝 或者两个一起用

由于 Hermes 使用 Python 而 OpenClaw 使用 Node.js，它们在运行时不冲突。你可以将不同频道路由到不同代理，用 OpenClaw 覆盖广泛的消息平台，同时用 Hermes 处理受益于其学习循环的深度工作任务。hermes claw migrate 工具支持你准备好时的渐进式迁移。

entry.title: Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw: Full Comparison
entry.content:
Hermes

vs🦞 OpenClaw

A comprehensive comparison from every perspective — architecture, security, memory, skills, platforms, cost, and more.
Updated April 2026

01 Origins & Philosophy02 Architecture03 Learning & Self-Improvement04 Memory Systems05 Skills Ecosystem06 Messaging Platforms07 Model Support08 Security09 Deployment & Infrastructure10 Developer Experience11 Cost Analysis12 Community & Ecosystem13 Enterprise & Team Use14 Research Capabilities15 Migration Path16 Final Verdict

01 Origins & Philosophy

Fig 1: Two fundamentally different bets on what an AI agent should prioritize.

OpenClaw defined the personal AI agent category. Originally called Clawdbot (Nov 2025), it was renamed Moltbot and then OpenClaw after trademark concerns. Creator Peter Steinberger joined OpenAI in February 2026, and the project moved to community governance under a non-profit foundation.

Hermes Agent arrived two months later from Nous Research — the lab behind the Hermes, Nomos, and Psyche model families. Where OpenClaw optimized for connecting to as many platforms and tools as possible, Hermes optimized for depth: making the agent genuinely learn and improve through use.

02 Architecture

Fig 2: Hermes centers on the agent loop; OpenClaw centers on the gateway control plane.
Aspect Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
CoreAIAgent loop (Python, ~9,200 lines)Gateway control plane (Node.js/TS)
Entry pointshermes (CLI) + hermes gatewayopenclaw CLI + Gateway daemon
State storageSQLite + FTS5 + flat filesJSON config + workspace files
ProtocolDirect LLM API callsWebSocket control plane
Plugin modelPython tools + MCP serversNode.js skills + ClawHub registry
CodebasePython (primary)Node.js / TypeScript

03 Learning & Self-Improvement HERMES WINS

This is the single biggest differentiator. Hermes has a closed learning loop that no other agent framework replicates. OpenClaw skills are static — you write them, they stay the same forever unless you manually update them.

Fig 3: Hermes creates and refines skills autonomously; OpenClaw relies entirely on human-authored static skills.
Capability Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
Skill creationAutonomous after complex tasks (5+ tool calls)Manual only (human writes SKILL.md)
Skill improvementSelf-improving during useNone (static files)
User modelingHoncho dialectic modeling across sessionsSOUL.md static identity file
Periodic nudgesAgent prompted to reflect and persistNo equivalent
Cross-session recallFTS5 search + LLM summarizationPersistent memory per assistant
Reported improvement40% speed improvement on repeated tasksNo compounding effect

04 Memory Systems HERMES WINS

Layer Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
Persistent factsMEMORY.md (~2,200 chars, frozen at session start)Per-assistant memory storage
User profileUSER.md (preferences, style)SOUL.md (identity & personality)
ProceduralSkills library (auto-created, searchable)Skills (human-authored, static)
EpisodicSQLite + FTS5 full-text search, unlimitedSession persistence per assistant
SummarizationLLM-powered summarization of past sessionsNo equivalent
External providers7 pluggable providers (Hindsight, PLUR, etc.)No pluggable memory system
Context compressionLossy summarization engine (pluggable)Context management via Gateway
Prompt cachingAnthropic prefix caching, frozen snapshotProvider-specific caching
Team sharingPLUR engrams across instancesPer-assistant isolation (built-in)

Hermes treats memory as a layered system: always-in-context facts, on-demand procedural skills, and searchable episodic history. OpenClaw's memory is simpler but effective for team isolation — each assistant has its own separate storage, preventing cross-contamination in multi-agent setups.

05 Skills Ecosystem OPENCLAW WINS

Aspect Hermes🦞 OpenClaw
Total skills70+ bundled, growing community13,700+ on ClawHub (44K reported)
Skill formatagentskills.io open standard (Markdown)Custom SKILL.md format (Markdown + scripts)
Skill sourceAuto-created by agent + community + Skills HubHuman-authored + ClawHub marketplace
LoadingProgressive disclosure (L0/L1/L2)Loaded at startup
Self-improvementSkills evolve during useStatic once written
Supply chain riskTirith pre-scan + --force for third-partyHigh — 1,467+ malicious skills found (ClawHavoc)
VettingScan verdicts block dangerous skills by defaultVirusTotal scanning (added post-crisis), minimal early vetting

OpenClaw's ecosystem is far larger in raw numbers. ClawHub has thousands of community skills covering everything from Gmail to Kubernetes. But that scale came with severe security costs — the ClawHavoc supply chain attack and 1,467+ confirmed malicious skills represent a serious trust problem. Hermes trades breadth for safety: fewer skills, but with pre-execution scanning and a safer default posture.

06 Messaging Platform Support OPENCLAW WINS

Fig 4: OpenClaw covers ~25 platforms; Hermes covers 15+ with deeper integration per platform.

OpenClaw has LINE, Google Chat, Microsoft Teams, IRC, Twitch, Nostr, Zalo, and native iOS/Android/macOS companion apps — none of which Hermes currently supports. Hermes's advantage is cross-platform conversation continuity with semantic context restore, and deeper per-platform integration (Discord voice channels, Telegram webhook mode, WeCom WebSocket).

07 Model Support HERMES WINS

Aspect Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

OpenRouter200+ models via unified billingSupported
Local modelsOllama, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cppOllama + custom endpoints
China providersMiniMax, Kimi/Moonshot, z.ai/GLM, DashScope, XiaomiLimited
MiniMaxFirst-class partner (M2.7 direct integration)Via OpenRouter

Fallback modelAuto-fallback mid-session on errorNo automatic fallback
Per-agent routingSingle model + fallbackDifferent models per agent
Minimum context64K tokens requiredNo enforced minimum
Auxiliary LLMSeparate model for vision, summarizationUses primary model

08 Security HERMES WINS

This is where the comparison becomes most stark. OpenClaw has faced one of the most significant AI security crises of 2026.

Important context: Hermes is younger and has a smaller attack surface (64K stars vs 345K). It hasn't faced the same level of scrutiny. However, its safer-by-default architectural decisions — Docker hardening as defaults rather than options, mandatory pre-scan of third-party skills, memory injection scanning — represent a fundamentally more security-conscious design.

11 Cost Analysis HERMES WINS

Component Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

Hermes's serverless backends (Modal, Daytona) give it a significant cost edge for users who don't need their agent running 24/7. If your agent runs 8 hours/day, you pay for 8 hours instead of 24.

12 Community & Ecosystem OPENCLAW WINS

Metric Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

OpenClaw's community is the largest in the AI agent space. The sheer volume of tutorials, third-party hosting providers, skills, and integrations creates a network effect. However, Hermes is growing at a pace that suggests it could challenge OpenClaw within a year — especially as developers migrate due to security concerns.

13 Enterprise & Team Use OPENCLAW WINS

Feature Hermes🦞 OpenClaw

14 Research Capabilities HERMES WINS

RL trainingAtropos RL environmentsNo RL infrastructure

Hermes was built by a model training lab. It's designed from the ground up as research infrastructure — not just a user-facing product. OpenClaw has no equivalent research capabilities.

15 Migration Path

OpenClaw → Hermes: Built-in Migration Tool

hermes claw migrate imports your persona (SOUL.md), memory, skills (auto-converted to agentskills.io), messaging configs, API keys, and TTS assets. Interactive preview with dry-run support. Skill conflicts are handled with skip/overwrite/rename options. You can run both agents side by side during transition.

🦞 Hermes → OpenClaw: Manual Process

No built-in migration tool. Requires manual mapping of memory files, skill format conversion, and channel reconfiguration. The self-improving skills system has no OpenClaw equivalent — you lose compounding automation value. Estimated effort: 12–21 hours.

16 Final Verdict

Fig 5: Category-by-category winner summary across all 14 comparison dimensions.

Choose Hermes When You...

  • Want an agent that genuinely improves over time
  • Prioritize security (zero CVEs, Docker hardened defaults)
  • Need deep memory across months of interactions
  • Want serverless deployment with near-zero idle costs
  • Work with Chinese LLM providers (MiniMax, GLM, Kimi)
  • Are a researcher needing RL training / trajectory generation
  • Want to migrate from OpenClaw (built-in migration tool)

🦞 Choose OpenClaw When You...

  • Need the broadest possible platform coverage (25+)
  • Want a massive skills ecosystem (13,700+ on ClawHub)
  • Need enterprise support (NVIDIA NemoClaw)
  • Require native Windows support
  • Want companion apps (macOS, iOS, Android)
  • Need multi-agent routing with per-assistant isolation
  • Already have an established OpenClaw deployment
🤝 Or Run Both

Since Hermes uses Python and OpenClaw uses Node.js, they don't conflict at runtime. You can route different channels to different agents, use OpenClaw for broad messaging coverage while Hermes handles deep-work tasks that benefit from its learning loop. The hermes claw migrate tool supports gradual migration when you're ready.

Sources: Hermes Agent GitHub · Hermes Official Docs · OpenClaw Official Docs · ARMO Security Research · Endor Labs · Sangfor Technologies · Koi Security Research

entry.title: Deep Dive into Redis VI: Redis vs ZooKeeper vs etcd
entry.summary: A Deep, Conceptual Comparison for Distributed Systems
entry.content:
A Deep, Conceptual Comparison for Distributed Systems​

1. High-Level Positioning​

SystemCore IdentityPrimary Purpose
RedisIn-memory data platformFast data access, caching, counters, queues
ZooKeeperDistributed coordination serviceStrong consistency, coordination, metadata
etcdDistributed key-value storeCluster configuration & service discovery

One Sentence Summary​

  • Redis: “Give me data now.”
  • ZooKeeper: “Coordinate distributed systems safely.”
  • etcd: “Store and watch cluster state consistently.”

2. Fundamental Design Philosophy​

Redis Philosophy​

Speed > Everything
Memory-first
Eventual consistency (cluster)
Application-driven logic

Redis optimizes for latency and throughput.

ZooKeeper Philosophy​

Correctness > Performance
Strong consistency
Coordination first
Centralized control plane

ZooKeeper optimizes for correct distributed behavior.

etcd Philosophy​

Simplicity + Consistency
Raft-based consensus
Cloud-native control plane
Observability-friendly

etcd optimizes for operational clarity and reliability.

3. Core Architecture Comparison​

Redis Architecture (Cluster Mode)​

               Client
                 |
     ┌───────────┴────────┐
     │     Redis Cluster  │
     └───────────┬────────┘
     ┌───────────┴───────────┐
┌────┴────┐ ┌────┴────┐ ┌────┴────┐
│ Master1 │ │ Master2 │ │ Master3 │
└────┬────┘ └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘
     │           │           │
  Replicas    Replicas    Replicas

Key points:

  • Hash slots (16,384)
  • Sharding for scale
  • Replication for availability
  • Not consensus-based

ZooKeeper Architecture​

            Client
                |
       ┌────────┴──────────┐
       │ ZooKeeper Quorum  │
       └────────┬──────────┘
     ┌──────────┼──────────┐
┌────┴────┐┌────┴────┐┌────┴────┐
│ Leader  ││Follower ││Follower │
└─────────┘└─────────┘└─────────┘

Key points:

  • Single leader
  • Zab protocol
  • Linearizable writes
  • Hierarchical namespace

etcd Architecture​

            Client
                |
       ┌────────┴────────┐
       │ etcd Cluster    │
       └────────┬────────┘
     ┌──────────┼──────────┐
┌────┴────┐┌────┴────┐┌────┴────┐
│ Leader  ││ Follower││ Follower│
└─────────┘└─────────┘└─────────┘

Key points:

  • Raft consensus
  • Strong consistency
  • Flat key-value space
  • Watch-based design

4. Consistency Model (Critical Difference)​

FeatureRedisZooKeeperetcd
ConsistencyEventualStrongStrong
Consensus❌ZabRaft
Split-brainPossiblePreventedPrevented
Linearizable writes❌✅✅

Visual Consistency Comparison​

Redis:
Write → Master → Async replicas
      (possible stale reads)

ZooKeeper / etcd:
Write → Leader → Majority ACK → Commit
      (always consistent)

5. Data Model Comparison​

Redis Data Model​

Key → Value
      ├── String
      ├── Hash
      ├── List
      ├── Set
      ├── ZSet
      └── Stream

Optimized for application data structures.

ZooKeeper Data Model​

/
├── app
│   ├── leader
│   ├── config
│   └── locks
  • Tree-like (filesystem style)
  • Znodes (small metadata)
  • Ephemeral nodes

etcd Data Model​

/services/app1/instances/1
/services/app1/instances/2
/config/db/timeout
  • Flat KV
  • Prefix-based grouping
  • First-class WATCH support

6. Failure Handling​

Redis Failure Model​

Master crashes
   ↓
Replica promoted
   ↓
Possible data loss window
  • Fast
  • Not transactional
  • Best-effort durability

ZooKeeper Failure Model​

Leader crashes
   ↓
Election
   ↓
New leader with consistent state
  • No data loss (committed)
  • Slower failover
  • Strong correctness

etcd Failure Model​

Leader crashes
   ↓
Raft election
   ↓
New leader
  • Guaranteed state safety
  • Designed for automation

7. Persistence & Storage​

AspectRedisZooKeeperetcd
Primary storageRAMDiskDisk
PersistenceRDB / AOFWAL + snapshotWAL + snapshot
Data volumeLargeSmallMedium
Restart recoveryFastModerateModerate

Redis Persistence​

RAM
 │
 ├─ RDB (snapshot)
 └─ AOF (append)

ZooKeeper / etcd Persistence​

Client writes
     ↓
WAL (log)
     ↓
Snapshot

8. Typical Use Cases (MOST IMPORTANT)​

Redis – When You SHOULD Use It​

✔ Caching
✔ Rate limiting
✔ Distributed counters
✔ Session storage
✔ Queues / Streams
✔ Real-time analytics
✔ Leaderboards

Diagram:

User → App → Redis → Response (sub-ms)

ZooKeeper – When You SHOULD Use It​

✔ Leader election
✔ Distributed locks
✔ Metadata management
✔ Kafka / HBase coordination
✔ Strong ordering guarantees

Diagram:

Services → ZooKeeper → Coordination

etcd – When You SHOULD Use It​

✔ Kubernetes state
✔ Service discovery
✔ Feature flags
✔ Distributed config
✔ Cloud-native control planes

Diagram:

Nodes → etcd → Watch → React

9. Watch / Notification Capability​

FeatureRedisZooKeeperetcd
WatchPub/SubWatcherNative Watch
ReliabilityBest-effortStrongStrong
Replay❌❌✅

etcd Watch Model​

Client sets watch
     ↓
Key changes
     ↓
Guaranteed event delivery

10. Scalability Characteristics​

AspectRedisZooKeeperetcd
Horizontal scaleExcellentPoorLimited
Data sizeVery largeVery smallSmall-medium
ClientsMillionsThousandsThousands

Why ZooKeeper Does NOT Scale Like Redis​

All writes → Leader
All coordination → Leader

This is intentional.

11. Operational Complexity​

AspectRedisZooKeeperetcd
SetupEasyHardMedium
DebuggingMediumHardMedium
TuningMany knobsMany knobsFew knobs
Cloud-nativePartialNoYes

12. Security & Access Control​

FeatureRedisZooKeeperetcd
AuthACL / AUTHACLTLS + RBAC
EncryptionTLSTLSTLS
Multi-tenancyLimitedLimitedStrong

13. What NOT to Do (Very Important)​

❌ Do NOT use Redis for:​

  • Distributed locks requiring strict correctness
  • Leader election with safety guarantees
  • Source of truth metadata

❌ Do NOT use ZooKeeper for:​

  • Large datasets
  • High-QPS application reads
  • Caching

❌ Do NOT use etcd for:​

  • Hot data paths
  • Large object storage
  • High-frequency counters

14. Decision Matrix (Quick Guide)​

Need speed? ───────────▶ Redis
Need correctness? ─────▶ ZooKeeper
Need cloud control? ───▶ etcd

15. Mental Model Summary​

Redis     = Data Plane
ZooKeeper = Coordination Plane
etcd      = Control Plane

They complement, not replace, each other.

16. Final Takeaway​

  • Redis is fast but not authoritative
  • ZooKeeper is authoritative but heavy
  • etcd is authoritative and cloud-native

The best systems often use all three, each for what it does best.
